title: The ten martyrs
hook: a Yom Kippur poem remembers ten sages killed by Rome

segments.voice: Yesterday, echad: Rabbi Akiva said the Shema to the end and died on the word one. Your line was with all your soul. Today, Akiva is remembered again, in a poem, with nine others.

It's Yom Kippur. People have been fasting since the evening before. In the additional service, called Musaf, the room goes quiet for a long poem. It opens with two Hebrew words, eleh ezkerah: these I remember. Then it tells, one by one, how Roman authorities put ten sages to death. The words echo a psalm: "These things I remember, and pour out my soul within me." On the Day of Atonement, in the middle of asking for forgiveness, the congregation stops to remember.
screen: `YOM KIPPUR, THE ADDITIONAL SERVICE.` → `ELEH EZKERAH: THESE I REMEMBER.` → `TEN SAGES, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: The poem frames it as a single decree. A Roman ruler reads in the Torah that kidnapping a person and selling him is a crime punished by death, and he remembers that Joseph's brothers sold Joseph. Since the brothers are long gone, he demands ten sages in their place. Rabbi Yishmael, the poem says, purifies himself and ascends to heaven to ask whether the decree truly comes from above, and he is told to accept it. Then the names. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Rabbi Yishmael. Rabbi Akiva, whose death we heard yesterday. Rabbi Chanina ben Teradion, who taught Torah in public with a scroll in his lap. The Talmud, in tractate Avodah Zarah, tells that he was burned wrapped in that scroll. His students asked what he saw, and he answered, in paraphrase: the parchment is burning, and the letters are flying up into the air. Some readers point out that the rabbis' own stories place these deaths at different times, not on one day. The poem gathers them anyway. It isn't a court record. It's a liturgy of memory, setting ten people in a row so a congregation can hold them together. A related lament is also said on the ninth of Av. And on Yom Kippur, the remembering sits inside the prayer, not beside it.
screen: `ONE DECREE, TEN SAGES.` · `RABBI YISHMAEL ASKS HEAVEN WHY.` · then, large: `THE PARCHMENT BURNS, THE LETTERS FLY.` · then: `THE POEM GATHERS THEM TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Choose someone, from any time or place, who was killed for what they believed or for teaching it; you may know a name, or only a story. Say the name quietly if you have one, or where it happened if you don't, and rest with the image of letters rising: what they taught, still in the air. If you pray, you can say a psalm you know in their memory.
Eleh ezkerah. These I remember, the Yom Kippur poem that names ten sages killed by Rome, among them Akiva and Chanina ben Teradion.
Your line: the ten. Ten names, held together in one poem. That's day nine hundred five.

howItsDone: In synagogues, the poem Eleh Ezkerah is read during the Yom Kippur Musaf service, and a related lament for the martyred sages is said on Tisha B'Av.

chat.says: Why stop in the middle of Yom Kippur to tell how ten rabbis were killed?
options: It's a liturgy of memory: the poem sets ten sages in a row so people remember.
It's said so people fast harder, as a punishment for the ten deaths.
It's read to stir up anger at Rome, and isn't really part of the prayers.
